question: Between January and October 2026, 1 115 million tonnes of Russian grain transited through Latvia, three times more than in the same period in 2025. EU tariffs make imports prohibitive, yet transit to non-EU countries is still permitted. Estonia has banned the transit of Russian and Belarusian grain via a national sanction.

Lithuania will instead hold cargoes at Klaipėda from 16 November 2026 until origin tests clear them. Latvia’s government argues that only the EU may act, citing exclusive competence and potential claims of up to EUR 800 million. On 9 October 2026, the leaders of the EU’s Baltic Member States called for an EU-wide ban.
Without a clear legal answer, the debate has become a blame-shifting exercise between the national capitals and Brussels. 1.

In the light of Article 36 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, can a Member State prohibit such transit on public-security grounds and under what conditions, and does the EU’s exclusive competence for common commercial policy alter that assessment?
Does Directive 2012/34/EU1 or any other EU act oblige Member States to grant access to rail infrastructure for this transit?
Does the Commission intend to propose an EU-wide transit ban and, if so, when, or does it consider this a matter to be decided at national level?
Directive 2012/34/EU of 21 November 2012 establishing a single European railway area, (OJ L 343, 14.12.2012, p. 32, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2012/34/oj). 1
